title: What's this?
goal: Point to things around you, name them, ask yes/no questions with *ba*, and meet the marker *ang* — the most important word in the whole language.
bekal: tell *ito*, *iyan* and *iyon* apart by distance from the speaker
make yes/no questions by slipping in *ba*
use *ang* and *mga* to mark the thing being talked about

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Sa loob ng bahay
dialogs.intro: Budi has just walked into his rented room. Aling Nena, the landlady, shows him what's in the room one thing at a time.

lines.speaker: Aling Nena:
lines.text: Ito ang kwarto mo. Maliit, pero malinis.
lines.id: This is your room. Small, but clean.
lines.literal: this si room your. small, but clean.

lines.speaker: Aling Nena:
lines.text: Iyan ay bentilador. Mainit dito sa Maynila.
lines.id: That's a fan. It's hot here in Manila.
lines.literal: that is fan. hot here in Manila.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: At iyon po? Aparador ba iyon?
lines.id: And that one, ma'am? Is that a wardrobe?

lines.speaker: Aling Nena:
lines.text: Oo, aparador iyon. Nasa loob ang mga unan.
lines.id: Yes, that's a wardrobe. The pillows are inside.
lines.literal: yes, wardrobe that. located inside si plural pillow.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Salamat po. Ano ang tawag dito sa Tagalog?
lines.id: Thank you, ma'am. What do you call this in Tagalog?
lines.literal: thanks ma'am. what si call to-this in Tagalog?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ay, marami po bang lamok dito?
lines.id: Oh, are there a lot of mosquitoes here, ma'am?

lines.speaker: Aling Nena:
lines.text: Hindi naman. Pero mag-ingat ka pa rin.
lines.id: Not really. But still be careful.
lines.literal: not indeed. but take-care you still also.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Sige po. Malinis po ang kwarto. Salamat!
lines.id: Okay, ma'am. The room is clean. Thank you!
lines.literal: all-right ma'am. clean ma'am si room. thanks!

lines.speaker: Aling Nena:
lines.text: Walang anuman, iho. Magpahinga ka na.
lines.id: You're welcome, son. Go get some rest.
lines.literal: nothing anything, son. rest you now.

notes: **Three distances, not two.** English splits the world into "this" and "that". Tagalog splits it into three: *ito* (near me), *iyan* (near you), *iyon* (far from us both). Spanish and Japanese do the same, and English once did too — think of old "yon" in *yonder*.

**Ang marks the thing in the spotlight.** In *Ito ang kwarto mo*, the word *ang* attaches to *kwarto* and says: this is what we're talking about. Think of *ang* as a stage spotlight. All of Tagalog grammar revolves around this light, and from unit 10 on you'll see why.

**Mga makes things plural, and is pronounced mah-NGAH.** *Ang unan* = the pillow; *ang mga unan* = the pillows. The noun itself doesn't change — you simply add *mga* before it, like adding "the" plus an extra word.

**Ba turns a statement into a question.** *Aparador iyon* (that's a wardrobe) → *Aparador ba iyon?* (is that a wardrobe?). No reversing the order (no "is that…"), no question word. Just slip *ba* in after the first word, and your voice can stay flat.

**Iyan ay bentilador** uses *ay*, a formal linker that flips the sentence into English-style order (subject first). Aling Nena uses it because she's explaining carefully. In fast conversation people say *Bentilador iyan* — and that's the one to imitate.

**Adjectives come first.** *Maliit ang kwarto*, not *ang kwarto maliit*. It's the same pattern as *Guro ako* in unit 1: the description in front, what it describes behind. You'll repeat this pattern hundreds of times.

**Hindi naman** is a gentle way to say "not really" or "not particularly". *Naman* softens almost anything it touches — refusing, correcting, comparing. Without *naman*, a bare *hindi* sounds firm and a bit cold.
**Iho** (from Spanish *hijo*, son) is used by older people to a young man; for a girl it's *iha*. The word is warm, not condescending — like "dear" or "son" from an older neighbor.

**Aling** before a woman's name (and *Mang* for a man) is a respectful address for an older person in the neighborhood: *Aling Nena*, *Mang Kanor*. The nearest English feel is "Mrs." and "Mr." said in a friendly village way.

grammars.title: Ito, iyan, iyon — three distances
body: Tagalog demonstratives come in three sets of forms, and this unit sets up the first one — the *ang* set, used when the pointer word is the spotlight of the sentence.

head: Form
Say it
Distance
Example
rows: Ano iyan? — What is that? (the one you're holding)
Ano iyon? — What is that? (the one over there)
Ilagay mo diyan. — Put it there.
Doon ang palengke. — The market is over there.

after: In fast speech, *iyan* and *iyon* are often shortened to *yan* and *yun* (written *'yan*, *'yun*). You'll hear these short forms more often than the long ones.
*Ito* is also used to introduce people: *Ito si Ana* — "this is Ana". Notice the marker changes to *si* because what's pointed at is a person's name.
The second set (*nito*, *niyan*, *niyon*) and how to use it comes in unit 5, after all three markers are in place.

grammars.title: Ang and mga — the spotlight and the plural marker
body: *Ang* is the most frequent word in Tagalog and also the hardest to translate: it isn't "that", it isn't "the" exactly. Its job is to mark **which thing is the spotlight of the sentence**.
after: **For people's names, *ang* becomes *si*** (one person) or *sina* (several people). It's mandatory and can't be skipped: *Guro Ana* sounds as wrong to a Filipino ear as "going Jakarta" without "to" does to ours.
**Mga always stands after its marker**, never alone at the start of a sentence: *ang mga bata*, *ng mga bata*, *sa mga bata*.
Nouns with no marker at all also appear often — *Guro ako*, *Bentilador iyan*. In this pattern the noun is acting as a description, not as the spotlight. The spotlight is *ako* and *iyan*.

blocks.text: Most Tagalog household nouns come from Spanish, so if you know any Spanish many of them will feel familiar right away.

blocks.title: Words you may already know
items: *Bintana* from *ventana*, *baso* from *vaso*, *kutsara* from *cuchara*: the **v becomes b** and **c becomes k** patterns from the pronunciation page are at work here.
*Kusina* (kitchen) is a cousin of English "cuisine" and Spanish *cocina*. *Silya* comes from Spanish *silla* — the same word, respelled the way Tagalog speakers say it.

blocks.text: Yes/no questions in Tagalog are made with one small word slipped into the sentence, not by reversing the word order as English does.

head: Statement
Question
Meaning
rows: Are there a lot of mosquitoes?

blocks.text: Notice the third row: if the sentence contains *ka*, *ko* or *mo*, those short words **come before** *ba*. The order among particles has its own rules, covered in full in unit 14. For now just memorize the forms *ka ba*, *mo ba*, *ko ba*.

Answering is short: *Oo* or *Hindi*, with *po* if you're being polite. To be clear, repeat the key word: *Oo, guro siya.* — *Hindi, hindi siya guro.* Notice that *hindi* appears twice: once as the answer, once as the negation of the sentence.

blocks.title: Ba is not a politeness marker
items: A question without *ba* is still correct if your voice rises: *Guro siya?* But in writing and in clear conversation, *ba* is far more usual.
Don't confuse it with English "ba" sounds or baby talk. This is a real function word and is required in almost every yes/no question.
There are a lot of mosquitoes.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the right pointer word: ito, iyan, iyon, dito, doon.
items: Ano ____? (an object in your own hand)
Ano ____? (an object the listener is holding)
Mainit ____. (in the place where you're standing)
____ si Ana. (introducing the person next to you)
